[[File:Extremenotexposed.png|thumb|The two distinguished points are examples of [[extreme point]]s of a convex set that are {{em|not}} exposed]]

In mathematics, an '''exposed point''' of a [[convex set]] <math>C</math> is a point <math>x\in C</math> at which some [[continuous linear functional]] attains its strict [[maximum]] over <math>C</math>.<ref>{{cite book | last = Simon| first = Barry| authorlink = Barry Simon| title = Convexity: An Analytic Viewpoint| publisher = Cambridge University Press| series = | chapter = 8. Extreme points and the Krein–Milman theorem| chapter-url = http://www.math.caltech.edu/Simon_Chp8.pdf| volume = | edition = | date = June 2011| location = | pages = 122| language = | url = | doi = | id = | isbn = 9781107007314| mr = | zbl = | jfm = }}</ref> Such a functional is then said to ''expose'' <math>x</math>. There can be many exposing functionals for <math>x</math>. The set of exposed points of <math>C</math> is usually denoted <math>\exp(C)</math>.

A stronger notion is that of ''strongly exposed point'' of <math>C</math> which is an exposed point <math>x \in C</math> such that some exposing functional <math>f</math> of <math>x</math> attains its strong maximum over <math>C</math> at <math>x</math>, i.e. for each sequence <math>(x_n) \subset C</math> we have the following implication: <math>f(x_n) \to \max f(C) \Longrightarrow \|x_n -x\| \to 0</math>. The set of all strongly exposed points of <math>C</math> is usually denoted <math>\operatorname{str}\exp(C)</math>.

There are two weaker notions, that of [[extreme point]] and that of [[support point]] of <math>C</math>.
